title: Echo Words
statement: Two words *echo* each other if one becomes the other by repeatedly moving its first letter to the end. For example, `"lamp"` echoes `"ampl"`, `"mpla"`, and `"plam"`, and every word echoes itself. Words of different lengths never echo.
Given a list of words, return how many groups of mutually echoing words there are.

examples.explanation: "lamp", "mpla", and "ampl" form one group. "palm" uses the same letters but isn't a rotation of "lamp", and neither is "lmap".

constraints: words consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every pair of words is slow. Can you give every word in a group the same key?
Pick one rotation to stand for the whole group, for example the alphabetically smallest one.
A word has only as many rotations as letters. Take the smallest one as the key and count distinct keys in a set.
pitfalls: Using the sorted letters as the key, which groups anagrams instead of rotations.
Counting duplicate words as separate groups.
Checking every pair with the doubled-string trick, which is correct but quadratic in the number of words.
interviewerNotes: If they reach for sorted letters, ask them to check "palm" against "lamp".
Ask why a canonical key turns a pairwise problem into a counting problem.
L is at most 20 here, so trying every rotation is fine. Strong candidates may mention Booth's algorithm or Lyndon words for linear-time minimal rotation.
